Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient was also directly physically injured; that direct-injury theme is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Threat items center on personal physical danger and hypervigilance in the environment ('back to wall', exaggerated startle), which fits direct personal assault/combat trauma more than trauma to a loved one, and is not well linked to the reported appraisal content.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, this item implies an ongoing need to guard against immediate external danger to oneself. That does not fit well with the rest of the profile, which centers on bereavement-related cognitions (survival guilt, numbness) rather than personal threat exposure. It is also weakly aligned with the formulation, where Threat is linked mainly with Negative Appraisals and not with trigger-driven hyperarousal or ongoing danger monitoring.

The threat items are dominated by nonspecific hyperarousal and reminder reactivity, which usually implies trigger-linked activation, but the formulation specifies Triggers → Threat as inactive. With no trigger content present, 'physical reactions when reminded' is poorly aligned with the stated formulation structure.

'Mistrust: People can't be trusted' is a broad interpersonal appraisal that is not well anchored to trauma to a loved one in the rest of this profile. The other appraisal items center on guilt and emotional deadness, but pervasive mistrust suggests a different trauma pattern and lacks support from the selected threat items.

vignette:
Bao has spent fifty of his sixty years on the water, reading the tides and the sky like a language he was born knowing. For the last six months, however, he has not set foot on a boat. The trauma did not happen to him, but to his nephew, Minh, who was learning the trade at his side. It was a day that had started like any other, the sun sharp on the calm Gulf waters. The squall came out of nowhere, a sudden darkening of the sky and a violent shift in the wind that Bao, for all his experience, didn't see coming until it was on them. He remembers the sickening lurch as the first wave crashed over the gunwale, the roar of the wind that swallowed his shouts to Minh, and the final, terrible groan of the boat as it surrendered to the sea. He clung to the overturned hull for hours, the cold seeping into his bones, but Minh was gone. A Coast Guard cutter found him at dusk, alone.

In the weeks that followed, the sea he had loved became his tormentor. Sleep offered no escape; he would lie awake for hours, the sound of the wind and crashing waves replaying in his mind until he was certain a storm was raging outside his bedroom window. When he did drift off, he would be jolted awake, heart hammering against his ribs, the feeling of icy water closing over him. During the day, the triggers were everywhere in his small fishing community. The smell of diesel from a boat engine starting up at the docks would send a wave of nausea through him and make his hands tremble. He would feel a cold sweat prickle his skin at the cry of a gull, the same sound that had echoed across the water as he floated, waiting. These were not just memories but physical assaults, his body reacting with a terror that left him breathless and ashamed of his own weakness.

A profound sense of guilt settled over him, a constant, low hum beneath the surface of his thoughts. He was the elder, the experienced one. He should have known, should have turned back, should have held on tighter to Minh. The question of why he survived when a boy with his whole life ahead of him did not became an unanswerable, crushing weight. He felt guilty for every breath he took, for the warmth of the sun on his face, for the simple fact of his own existence. This guilt curdled into a deep-seated mistrust of others. When neighbours and fellow fishermen would offer condolences, he heard only judgment in their hushed tones. He became certain they were blaming him, whispering about his failure behind his back. He came to believe that people's kindness was a mask for their morbid curiosity, and that no one could ever be trusted to understand the horror he carried.

This isolation has been compounded by a feeling he can only describe as being "dead inside." His wife, Ly, tries to reach him, holding his hand or cooking his favorite phở, but he feels nothing. The comfort of her touch is a distant pressure, the taste of the food is ash in his mouth. The vibrant life he once lived-the satisfaction of a full net, the easy camaraderie with other fishermen, the quiet love for his wife-has been replaced by a vast, hollow emptiness. He has not gone back out to sea, a decision that has strained their finances and, more profoundly, severed him from his own identity. He is a fisherman who cannot fish, a man adrift on dry land. It was Ly who finally made the appointment, her face etched with a fear he could not bring himself to feel. He agreed to come not out of hope, but out of a weary sense of obligation. What he fears most is that this internal deadness is permanent, that the man he was is as lost to the waves as his nephew.
